items.title: [phys.org] UN warns warming will breach 1.5C as COP31 opens Monday
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

The United Nations says global warming will exceed the 1.5-degree Celsius threshold as nearly 200 countries prepare to begin the COP31 climate talks in Antalya, Turkey, on Nov. 9. Climate scientists say the rate of warming has effectively doubled over the past decade. October 2026 was the hottest October on record, and 2026 is virtually certain to become the second year to exceed 1.5C, after 2024. U.N. Secretary-General António Guterres said the world must now limit how far temperatures rise beyond that level and blamed political leaders for failing to act. The Nov. 9-20 talks are expected to focus on fulfilling earlier promises to move away from fossil fuels and on funding for poorer countries facing climate impacts. Turkey is promoting a goal to increase electricity’s share of global energy demand from about 20% to 35% by 2035. Developed countries have resisted further funding commitments, and the Trump administration is not taking part in negotiations.

items.title: [cbc.ca] Parks Canada expects to eliminate about 500 full-time-equivalent positions, ends Banff rescue-dog program
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

Parks Canada expects to eliminate about 500 full-time-equivalent positions, close 13 park-warden detachments and discontinue its Banff search-and-rescue dog program as part of $145 million in cuts over three years. The agency sent workforce-adjustment notices to 2,917 employees and says it will make individual decisions in the coming weeks. The Canadian Avalanche Rescue Dog Association and British Columbia Search Dog Association have urged the agency to reverse the cancellation, warning it could weaken rescue capacity. Parks Canada says it will shift wardens to a regional model focused on high-risk areas and that wardens can enforce park law without dogs. The associations say they are working on a short-term volunteer response during avalanche season.

🪶 ✏️

Prime Minister Mark Carney announced a $1-billion federal commitment in Winnipeg on Friday for more than 2,000 supportive and transitional homes and a mental-health and addictions centre as part of the government’s 10-year homelessness plan. The package allocates $800 million to housing and $200 million to the centre and renovations at similar facilities; the centre’s location has not been chosen. The partners include Manitoba, Winnipeg, First Nations governments, community organizations and private funders. The Southern Chiefs’ Organization and True North Sports and Entertainment are among the partners, and Manitoba has committed $84 million annually to the effort. The announcement follows the federal budget’s national homelessness initiative, which Carney said requires co-ordination among governments and contributions from business and philanthropy.

items.title: [dagenslantbruk.se] Farmers urged to tailor grazing to grassland recovery and climate
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

Agricultural specialists in Sweden, France and South Africa say grassland management requires continued upkeep and grazing adapted to local vegetation and weather. Sweden’s inventory found that the natural and cultural values of most re-surveyed meadows and pastures remained broadly stable, while French livestock farmers discussed how the 2026 drought and heat affected forage production. University of Limpopo pasture scientist Lesego Motshekga says rotational grazing works only when stocking rates match available forage and plants have time to recover; moving animals between camps alone cannot prevent overgrazing. Motshekga recommends deciding when to move livestock based on grass condition rather than a fixed calendar.

items.title: [LoRaMeshDevices] DIY Meshtastic Solar Node: Muziworks Uno Full Build Guide
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

A bare Meshtastic board, a battery and a solar panel are a good start. To turn them into something I can leave outside, I want a proper enclosure, a secure mounting arrangement, an external antenna and sealed cable entries. For this build, I’m using the Elecrow Muziworks Muzi Base Uno. I already had the small solar panel wired up and the basic configuration working. Now I’m putting everything into a weatherproof case, updating the firmware and getting the node ready for an outdoor test. The big question is the solar panel. It is very small, and I’m not yet convinced it will keep the battery charged. This is a working build ready for testing, not a proven, indefinitely self-sufficient solar installation. Key Takeaways Update and verify the firmware before enclosing the board, while USB access is easy. Plan the internal layout around USB clearance, battery-connector access and safe assembly. Seal every new enclosure opening, including the solar-wire entry behind the panel. Successful mesh communication does not prove the small solar panel can sustain the node. Table of Contents Parts and Layout Update the Meshtastic Firmware First Make a Small 3D-Printed Board Mount Prepare the Enclosure and External Connections Mount the Board and Battery Route, Solder and Attach the Solar Panel Seal the Cable Entry and Check the Finished Layout Configure the Node for a Fixed Installation Run a Traceroute Before Mounting Outside Put It Outside and Test the Solar Side Parts and Layout The Uno does not have the Wi-Fi capability of the Duo, which suits what I want from this solar node. It also came with a small three-wire battery, including a sensing wire rather than just the usual positive and negative connections. Here is what I used: Muzi Base Uno and its supplied battery. A weatherproof enclosure with rear mounting hardware and an internal mounting plate. A small solar panel, already connected during the earlier setup. An SMA male to N female bulkhead adapter for the external antenna connection. A larger 915 MHz external antenna. A gasketed enclosure breather plug. A custom 3D-printed board mount, small screws, 3M double-sided mounting tape and silicone sealant. The linked parts are affiliate links, which means I may earn from qualifying purchases. Before fixing anything down, check the whole layout. The board needs room for its antenna connection, battery plug and solar wiring. Just as importantly, leave enough clearance to connect a USB cable for future firmware updates. A neat installation is not much use if you have to dismantle it every time you need access. Update the Meshtastic Firmware First I did the firmware update before putting the board in the enclosure. It is much easier to work with the USB connection while everything is still on the bench. Connect the antenna before powering the board. I kept that same order later when connecting the battery. Connect the Uno to the computer with a USB cable. Open the Meshtastic web flasher at flasher.meshtastic.org. Select Muziworks, then the Muzi Base Uno/Duo device entry. Select the firmware version and start the flashing process. Follow the prompt to put the nRF-based board into DFU mode. When the board appears as a removable drive, download the matching UF2 firmware file. Copy the UF2 file onto that drive and wait for the transfer to finish. I chose Meshtastic 2.8.2 alpha for this build. That was a deliberate choice to try the newer firmware, not a recommendation to treat an alpha release as stable. The flasher offered different release channels, so check what you are selecting rather than simply assuming the newest option is the best one. Before copying the new firmware over, I also saved a copy of the existing UF2 file from the device drive to my computer. That gave me a local copy of the old firmware. I would not treat that as a separate backup of all the device settings. Once the copy completed, the drive ejected and disappeared as the board restarted. I reconnected in the Meshtastic app and checked the device details. The firmware version now showed 2.8.2, which confirmed the update had worked. Take an Initial Noise Reading The newer firmware exposed an antenna noise reading that I wanted to try. With the little stock antenna attached, the app reported approximately -97 dBm and displayed the result in green. That gave me a useful starting point before changing the enclosure and antenna. It is a noise-floor reading, though, not a range test or a measurement of antenna gain. For noise, a more negative value means a lower noise level: -97 dBm is quieter than -83 dBm. Make a Small 3D-Printed Board Mount I like mounting the board on a small raised plate rather than fixing it directly against the bottom of the enclosure. It keeps the installation tidier and leaves some space underneath the components. For this one, I drew a basic sketch with the dimensions I needed and used AI to help turn it into a printable mount. The result was an STL file that I opened in the slicer, checked and printed in PETG. The mounting-hole spacing came out correctly, and the board fitted the printed part. I used three small screws to secure it. The printed mount is optional. What matters is keeping the board secure, clear of the enclosure floor and accessible enough to maintain. There was one detail I would improve in another version: make the battery connector easier to reach after the board is mounted. That became awkward during assembly. Prepare the Enclosure and External Connections I have used this style of enclosure on other outdoor nodes without problems, so it is a familiar starting point. The supplied brackets attach to the back for mounting against a wall or another support. The case also came with cable-entry fittings, but I did not need those for this layout. Instead, I made openings for: The antenna bulkhead at the top. The breather plug on the side. The solar-panel wires behind the panel. I drilled the antenna and breather openings first. The solar-wire hole came later in my assembly, although planning all the openings before installing the electronics would make the job simpler. Fit the Breather Plug The breather plug is there to help manage moisture inside the enclosure. I am not using it as a cooling vent. It passes through the side wall and tightens against a rubber gasket. I seated the gasket against the case and tightened the fitting so it sat securely. Fit the Antenna Bulkhead The antenna connection uses an SMA male to N female bulkhead arrangement. Check the actual connector contacts as well as the threads: in this build, the SMA pin mates with the socket on the board’s antenna connection. The bulkhead passes through the top of the enclosure and has its own rubber gasket. Tightening the retaining hardware compresses that gasket against the case. The antenna and breather fittings are in place before the electronics go into the case. I then fitted the larger 915 MHz antenna to the outside. The N connector gives me a substantial external connection rather than leaving the small board-level connection exposed. Mount the Board and Battery With the external fittings installed, I checked the internal layout again. I positioned the printed mount low enough in the case to preserve USB access, with the battery beside it and room to route the antenna and solar wiring. I used two strips of 3M double-sided tape beneath the printed mount. I have had good results with this tape on other outdoor builds, so I used it again for the mount, battery and panel. Getting the backing off the tape is usually the part that tests my patience. This time, it was not too bad. The more important difficulty was the battery connector. I initially had the board attached to the mount, then removed it again because I was bending the cable and making the assembly awkward to handle. With the mount fixed down, I connected the antenna, plugged in the battery and taped the battery into the middle of the case. Everything fitted, but reinstalling the board screws while it was powered made me uncomfortable. A dropped screw could short the board. That is the part of this assembly I would change: finish the screw work with power disconnected. A better connector-access cutout in the mount, or a suitable power switch, would make the build much easier to work on. There is no prize for trying to balance tiny screws over a live board. Route, Solder and Attach the Solar Panel The panel sits on the outside of the lid. To get its wires through the enclosure, I disconnected the panel leads, drilled a small hole behind its intended position and passed the wires through. I then soldered the leads back onto the panel, keeping positive and negative on their correct connections. Check the panel position against the lid. Route the wires through the opening behind the panel. Reconnect the positive and negative leads. Check that the wires and solder joints do not prevent the panel from sitting properly. Attach the panel with mounting tape. Seal the wire opening with silicone. I ran into a small problem here: the solder connection on the back of the panel stood proud enough to stop it sitting flat against the lid. The first two strips of tape did not provide enough clearance. I adjusted the mounting with additional tape so the panel could sit properly without rocking on the solder joint. It is worth checking that clearance before pressing the adhesive down firmly. The panel’s rating was not clearly established during this build, so I am not going to give it a definite wattage or current specification. It is simply a very small panel, and its ability to keep this node running still needs an outdoor test. Seal the Cable Entry and Check the Finished Layout The antenna bulkhead and breather plug have gaskets, but the solar-wire hole needs separate sealing. I used silicone around that opening to keep water from entering along the wires. The hole is behind the solar panel, which gives it some shelter, but that is not a substitute for sealing it. Before closing the lid, I checked the main items: The board and battery were secured. The antenna connection was attached. The solar leads were connected and routed inside the case. The USB port remained accessible. The external fittings were tightened and the wire entry was sealed. At this point, the node was assembled in an enclosure intended for outdoor use. That is different from having a verified waterproof rating for the modified build. The drilled openings and seals still need to hold up in practice. Configure the Node for a Fixed Installation Back in the Meshtastic app, I requested another noise reading with the external antenna connected. It returned approximately -97 dBm, much like the stock antenna reading on the bench. That was encouraging, but it did not demonstrate a range improvement. The node was still indoors, and a noise reading alone cannot tell me how well a rooftop installation will perform. I initially left the device in Client mode. For this fixed-node experiment, I then changed the role to Client Base, selected the option to rebroadcast everything and saved the settings. The node restarted and reappeared in the app. Those are the settings I chose for this installation, rather than a claim that every solar-powered Meshtastic node should use exactly the same configuration. Run a Traceroute Before Mounting Outside For a basic connectivity check, I tried a traceroute to a nearby node down the street. The request reached it directly, while the reply came back through a different path. That confirmed the assembled node could communicate on the mesh. I then stood the enclosure upright so the antenna was vertical instead of lying along the desk and repeated the test. The displayed link reading improved from roughly -11 dB to -9 dB. It was a useful reminder to test the antenna in its intended orientation, but it was still only a short bench check, not a measured outdoor range test. Put It Outside and Test the Solar Side For the first outdoor trial, I mounted the enclosure on the side of my garden shed. This is not its final position. I wanted an accessible place to see whether the whole assembly worked before moving it to a roof. The shed mount is a temporary test position before a possible roof installation. By then, the solar-panel mounting had been sorted out, the case was closed and the node was running. Firmware flashing, the external antenna connection and the initial mesh checks had all worked. The unresolved part is the energy budget. I need to leave it outside over the next few days and find out whether that little panel can keep up with the node’s consumption. For now, I have a tidy, enclosed Meshtastic solar-node build ready for that test. If the panel proves too small, that will be the next thing to change. Getting the hardware assembled is one milestone; proving that it can stay running outside is the next one.

items.title: [downtoearth.org.in] Cyclone Arnab stalls off India, prolonging rain and flood threat
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

Cyclone Arnab’s slow, near-stationary approach to India’s Andhra Pradesh coast prolonged the landfall process and heightened the risk of extreme rain and flash flooding, Down To Earth reported. The storm crossed the southeastern coast on Wednesday, Oct. 28, after forming over the Bay of Bengal. The India Meteorological Department (IMD) warned that its slow movement could keep drawing moisture from the sea. The weather bureau recorded 217 millimetres of rain in Visakhapatnam and warned of flash flooding across coastal Andhra Pradesh and nearby regions through late Wednesday. Several reports linked the unusually intense storm season to El Niño and warming. Swiss public broadcaster RTS also reported that scientists say climate change amplifies El Niño’s effects.

items.title: [theguardian.com] Ceasefire lets hundreds flee occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

Hundreds of civilians evacuated from Russian-occupied Oleshky reached Ukrainian-held territory on Saturday, Oct. 31, after a local ceasefire allowed them to leave and aid to enter. U.S. First Lady Melania Trump mediated the pause, while Pope Leo XIV urged access for aid and evacuations. The ceasefire began Tuesday in the southern Kherson region and was scheduled to end Sunday evening. Residents travelled by bus through occupied Crimea to Russia, then flew to Belarus and crossed into Ukraine’s Chernihiv region, where relatives and aid workers met them. Some evacuees said food supplies had run out and they had survived on garden plants. The ceasefire also allowed roads to be cleared of mines and food and medicine to enter Oleshky. Ukraine and Russia have not disclosed how many people left. Melania Trump said the convoy could safely evacuate more than 750 people; an estimated 1,700 remained in Oleshky before the operation. Russia’s human rights commissioner said both sides had agreed to continue humanitarian missions. The truce was set to expire Sunday night.

The ceasefire, brokered with help from U.S. first lady Melania Trump and supported by Pope Leo XIV, allowed food and medical supplies into the frontline town; officials have not confirmed the total number evacuated. People headed for Ukrainian-controlled areas were taken first to Anapa in southern Russia and were then due to fly to Belarus and travel by bus into Ukraine. The circuitous route avoids mined roads along the front line. More than 1,000 residents, many elderly, remained in the town, according to a report from the scene; they received food, medicine, hygiene supplies and fuel. The truce is due to end late Sunday, Nov. 1. The Russian and Ukrainian human rights commissioners have asked Melania Trump to help coordinate recurring relief missions, while peace talks involving Russia, Ukraine and the United States are expected to resume in Abu Dhabi in early November.

items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

The U.S. State Department on Friday approved a proposed $2.1 billion sale of 500 Patriot PAC-3 interceptors to Ukraine, subject to congressional review. Canada, Germany and Norway will contribute through JUMPSTART, a U.S. program that allows allies to fund arms purchases for Ukraine, alongside funds backed by the European Union’s Ukraine Support Loan. The State Department said no U.S. funds would be used. Lockheed Martin is the principal contractor. The authorization follows Ukrainian complaints that Washington had taken nearly a month to approve missile supplies as Russia intensified attacks on energy and civilian infrastructure. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy welcomed the approval but warned that deliveries of the newly manufactured interceptors could take years to begin. Two people briefed on the decision told Al Jazeera they did not expect deliveries until the early 2030s. Zelenskyy has urged the United States and European partners to transfer missiles from existing stockpiles now and replenish them later through the new order. The State Department did not provide a delivery schedule. Congress has received the proposed sale for a 30-day review.

items.title: [theguardian.com] UN-backed report warns overshooting 1.5C could permanently damage Earth's ice
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

A report by 80 scientists convened by the International Cryosphere Climate Initiative and the U.N. Environment Programme warns that even a temporary rise above the Paris Agreement’s 1.5C warming limit could cause lasting losses to glaciers, sea ice and polar ice sheets. Earth has already warmed about 1.3C from preindustrial levels. The authors say any period above 1.5C should be as brief as possible before temperatures fall much further, and identify a long-term target below 1C by 2150. Under current policies, warming is projected to reach about 2.8C, a level the report links to near-total thaw of near-surface permafrost and likely severe disruption to ocean circulation. Greenland and Antarctic ice sheets would continue losing ice even if temperatures later returned to 1.5C, while many ice systems could take centuries or millennia to recover. The report was released ahead of the COP31 climate conference in Turkey.

items.content_html:

Weather extremes damaged crops and forage across Europe and South Asia in 2026, with drought and heat reducing yields and a cold winter with little snow harming Sweden’s autumn-sown grains. France’s sunflower harvest was estimated at 1.2 million tonnes, 14% below 2025, while Boerenbond estimated €260 million in losses for Flemish farmers and growers. In Baden-Württemberg, summer rainfall totaled 156 mm, about 45% below the 1961-1990 average; the state farmers’ association estimated forage losses at 30% to 40%, reaching 50% in the worst-hit locations. In Maharashtra’s Shevgaon area, drought has reduced fodder availability, while mechanized sugarcane harvesting removes a traditional source of green feed. Farmers say their livestock are producing less milk. Following late-September rain, Baden-Württemberg farmers are assessing whether grassland has recovered and whether reseeded areas will need further repair after winter.

items.title: [abcnews.com] Swift telescope shutdown ends rapid alerts for cosmic explosions
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

NASA shut down its Swift Observatory in late October after it could no longer hold steady enough for observations, ending a 22-year mission to detect gamma-ray bursts, supernovas and other high-energy events. Swift’s rapid observations helped direct other space telescopes toward eruptions for more detailed study, and astronomers are working out how to replace that alert function. The observatory resumed observations after the rescue effort ended and captured additional gamma-ray bursts and other ultrahigh-energy events before NASA turned off its systems. Over its mission, Swift recorded more than 2,000 gamma-ray bursts and 1,400 exploding stars.
